name: PowerShell
summary: A cross-platform shell language and runtime that parses commands into executable representations, composes typed pipeline objects through command processors, exposes provider-backed session state, and can project execution into remoting runspaces.

features.name: Language parser and syntax tree
features.description: PowerShell parses input into tokens and syntax-tree representations before command execution, allowing language constructs, expressions, redirections, and command arguments to be represented separately from runtime invocation.
benefits: Separates language recognition from command execution
Provides structured syntax for diagnostics and tooling
costs: Language grammar and parsing rules are compatibility-sensitive
A richer syntax model increases runtime and tooling surface

features.name: Command processor and object pipeline
features.description: The runtime turns parsed commands into command processors and connects them through pipeline execution, passing .NET objects between commands rather than requiring text serialization at every stage.
benefits: Composes commands with structured object values
Makes parameter binding and command lifecycle explicit
costs: Command binding and adapter behavior can be difficult to predict
Object serialization is still required at native or remoting boundaries

features.name: Provider-backed session state
features.description: Execution context and session-state objects hold variables, functions, aliases, drives, providers, and other invocation state; providers project resources such as the filesystem into command-facing locations.
benefits: Unifies heterogeneous resources behind shell navigation and commands
Scopes state to explicit execution contexts and runspaces
costs: Provider behavior adds indirection over underlying resources
Session state lifetime and scope rules add language complexity

features.name: Remoting and runspace boundary
features.description: Runspace pools and remoting clients provide a separate execution boundary for remote pipelines, with connection, invocation, output, and teardown state coordinated outside the local command processor.
benefits: Reuses the shell execution model across local and remote targets
Makes remote concurrency and session lifetime explicit
costs: Transport, authentication, serialization, and remote failure become part of execution
Remote object behavior differs from in-process object behavior

mathematical_views.question: How does source text transition through tokens, syntax nodes, command processors, and pipeline output?
assumptions: Command processors consume and emit pipeline objects
Host presentation is outside the pipeline state

mathematical_views.question: How do runspaces contain scopes, commands, variables, drives, and provider projections?
assumptions: A runspace is an execution-state boundary
Scopes and providers expose typed resource relationships
The graph abstracts host-specific provider implementations

mathematical_views.question: Which pipeline operations cross from a local runspace into a remote execution session?
assumptions: Remoting requests are separately authorized transitions
The model does not prove deployment security

costs: Language grammar and parsing rules are compatibility-sensitive

benefits: Composes commands with structured object values
costs: Command binding and adapter behavior can be difficult to predict

benefits: Unifies heterogeneous resources behind shell navigation
costs: Provider behavior adds indirection over underlying resources

benefits: Reuses execution semantics across local and remote targets
costs: Transport and serialization add failure and compatibility modes
